speakers: Toby Crabel (founder, Crabel Capital Management, short-term systematic futures)
summary: April 2026 interview with Crabel on how edges vanish: opening range breakout decayed as 24-hour trading removed the open, markets show more reversals and big-trader liquidity taking, and the firm responds with 10% annual portfolio turnover, generalized balanced mean-reversion/momentum strategies, execution investment and volume-price (effort vs result) research.

coverage.note: cold open (humbling markets), intro and sponsor text, tennis to futures biography
early career, opening range breakout origins
ORB decay, 24-hour sessions, adding mean reversion, new reference points
reversals, liquidity moved to the close, Monroe Trout anecdote
evolving portfolios, market makers, 23 March 2026 gold and silver reversal
liquidity-taking by big traders, follow-through probability, volume
quantifying chart patterns, AI vs charts, high-frequency traders
order book depth, momentum decay and allocation response
shorter holds, generalized versus optimized strategies, execution as edge
slippage, AI coding, markets as non-linear, volume watch
replication, capacity, AI pattern recognition competition
philosophy of technical analysis, 1970s analogy, gold and trend
personal style, S&P pit edge decay, short-term preference

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: if the market moved eight ticks above or below the open, they would actually fade that and if it went beyond that, they would start to to go with it.
claims.claim: Opening range breakout, from Chicago bond floor traders who faded an 8-tick move off the open but followed beyond it, was the foundational short-term momentum edge the speaker built strategies on in the late 1980s.

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: opening range breakout is a great measure of momentum in markets which is a huge factor.
claims.claim: Opening range breakout is a measure of intraday momentum, a large factor; the speaker learned the opposing mean-reversion view from Niederhoffer and kept both.

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: trend days. Uh generally they're not as frequent it doesn't look like as they used to be. There seem there seem to be there seems to be uh a lot of liquidity against momentum
claims.claim: Trend days are less frequent than before because liquidity is positioned against momentum, pushing strategies toward mean reversion.
claims.testable: yes: count trend days over time

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: where is the open? I For God's sake, I mean you there's so much volume in the 24-hour sessions, it's impossible to determine what the open is.
claims.claim: Opening range breakout deteriorated (worst in decades in the last 2-3 years) because 24-hour trading removed the meaningful open as a reference point, a dissipation first seen in the 1980s with US Treasury night sessions.
claims.conditions: markets with a clear primary session still work (palm oil, Brazil)
claims.testable: yes: compare ORB in 24h versus session markets

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: the one thing that you know, I did in the '90s also with my portfolio after working with Victor was to add mean reversion to sort of offset
claims.claim: After working with Niederhoffer, the speaker added mean-reversion strategies in the 1990s to offset the expected decay of opening range breakout; the decay took 8-10 more years and is glacial.
claims.indicator: mean reversion added to momentum book
claims.testable: yes: combine mean-reversion and breakout books

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: Uh one is the close of the previous day and the movement off of that.
claims.claim: Replacement reference points for the open include the previous close and overnight movement, previous-day highs and lows and the 24-hour session range; they work, though less strongly than the old opening range.
claims.indicator: previous close, overnight move, previous-day high/low

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: many more reversals uh instead of follow-through days now than there have been in quite a while.
claims.claim: There are many more intraday reversals (new overnight lows followed by large rallies) and fewer follow-through days than in a long time.
claims.testable: yes: count reversals versus follow-through days

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: nowadays it's actually around the close.
claims.claim: Liquidity has migrated from the open to the close (stock index closing volume is high), making the close a more significant reference point than the open.

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: there's probably a 10% or more shift in our portfolios every year because of the the amount of work we're doing now.
claims.claim: Old portfolios do not work as well as current ones, and the firm changes 10% or more of its portfolio every year because markets evolve; without changes the 5-10 year old portfolio would have gone out of business.
claims.indicator: annual portfolio turnover of strategies about 10%
claims.testable: yes: rolling comparison of old versus current portfolio

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: the market makers now, they're all, you know, algorithmic um and they're huge. And um most of them are very profitable. And we work against them.
claims.claim: Large algorithmic market makers and big traders use activity beyond prior-day highs and lows to enter and exit, so volatile liquidity events are an opportunity for big traders and reversals are more common.
claims.indicator: previous-day highs and lows, volume spikes
claims.testable: partly: needs volume data by participant

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: five, 10 times more volume than typically.
claims.claim: On 23 March 2026 gold and silver fell and reversed on 5-10 times normal volume, with large contracts trading ten minutes before Iran-talk headlines; the speaker sees this as big players using fear-driven liquidation to buy.
claims.indicator: volume spike at lows in gold and silver
claims.direction: buy after high-volume low in a bull market

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: Big traders need liquidity. They need they need they need to get fed, so to speak, and the markets by trading through highs and lows provide that liquidity
claims.claim: Big traders need liquidity, and markets trading through highs and lows provide it from fearful traders liquidating, so breaks of obvious levels are often traps.
claims.indicator: breaks of prior highs and lows with volume

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: let's say that it used to be, you know, 62% of the time the market would follow through after it took out a higher low. Well, now it's only 58% of the time.
claims.claim: The probability of follow-through after a higher low was taken out fell from about 62% to 58%; a few percentage points of edge decay change the behaviour of markets materially.

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: there's huge interests that are taking advantage of liquidity pockets. Wherever that wherever that volume comes in, they that's, you know, their eyes open wide.
claims.claim: Large volume outside prior ranges signals opportunity for big players; volume is more important now than the speaker recalls, as seen in Wyckoff's 1930s study of the New York Times index in a volatile bear market.

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: The charts aren't really look I it's not like you there's a there's a a premise that we we have to hold to all the time.
claims.claim: Charts show what is going on; the firm quantifies visual observations to detect market changes, and the human mind still extracts information from charts better than a computer, so we still must tell the computer what to do.
claims.testable: partly: visual features can be quantified

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: the high frequency groups, you know, they really are the liquidity uh backbone of the markets.
claims.claim: High-frequency firms act like the old floor traders as the liquidity backbone and do not take alpha from short-term managers; they pay heavily for microsecond speed, while the firm invests in execution instead.

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: Well, you're lucky to get 20 now uh showing on the in the book.
claims.claim: S&P futures book depth fell from about 500 contracts to about 20 at the touch while volume rose, so execution is more cagey and splitting orders is needed.

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: there's been a deterioration in the momentum basic momentum strategies of 4 or 5% say say they're still successful uh above 50% or something like that
claims.claim: Basic momentum strategies have deteriorated by 4-5 points of hit rate (still above 50%) because options traders and pod groups compress volatility; the firm shifts allocation, front-loads adjustments and monitors each portfolio section by market.
claims.testable: yes: track hit rate decay by strategy

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: Our portfolio has gone from probably an average of 36-hour hold to something less than
claims.claim: Markets are news-prone and jumpy, so the short-term program's average hold has shortened from about 36 hours to less.

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: late in the late '90s I decided to generalize uh the strategies into a portfolio of six primary mean reversion strategies and six primary uh momentum strategies
claims.claim: Portfolio of six uncorrelated mean-reversion and six momentum general strategies with balanced weight; four of the top five performers that year were the generalized ones even though optimized strategies looked better on paper.
claims.testable: yes: compare general versus optimized versions

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: if you optimize too much, you're fooling yourself in this in this systematic area.
claims.claim: Over-optimization is self-deception; generalized strategies hold up (some 1990s strategies still run), and the speaker looks for strategies that could last 50 years.
claims.testable: yes: out-of-sample decay of optimized vs general

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: I think we're kind of in a '70s environment.
claims.claim: Markets are as tough as in 40-50 years; there is a '70s-like environment but with an unidentified further factor causing challenges.

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: you have to get better at execution. Find ways of doing something that don't cost you
claims.claim: Execution is a main source of edge: execution quality has improved by multiples in 20-25 years and slippage is at the best level in the firm's history.

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: Watch out for extraordinary volume. At any point of the day.
claims.claim: Extraordinary volume at any point of the day, especially at the start of a regional session, is a signal worth watching.

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: you've got to expect that anything can happen. Anything can happen in the markets.
claims.claim: Markets are non-linear and only probabilistic, so AI cannot give a reliable 5-minute forecast and anything can happen; the mood among systematic and discretionary traders is humility.

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: we look at our dollars per contract net and we look at what it's costing us to actually execute. And if there's not a fair margin there
claims.claim: Capacity is assessed by net dollars per contract against execution cost; if the margin is thin there is a problem, and this matters far more for very short-term than 5-10 day holds.
claims.indicator: net dollars per contract, execution cost

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: there's enough nuance and interesting elements about it that it's going to be very it's going to be hard to replicate. That's why it's a higher cost product.
claims.claim: Short-term strategies are hard to replicate because of nuance and heavy execution investment; trend following products are easier to replicate but the firm's version has done slightly better.

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: speed and uh ability to quantify data is really what what what it's all about.
claims.claim: AI and genetic algorithms accelerate quantification, so short-term trading becomes more competitive as everyone uses every tool.

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: volume itself and the relationships of volume to price is a subject that I think a lot of people have overlooked.
claims.claim: The relationship between volume and price is under-researched; many stick to price alone and miss nuance, and a deep database remains unexplored.
claims.testable: yes: add volume features to price models

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: Effort is volume and the result is the position of the price range, the size of the price range
claims.claim: Wyckoff's effort versus result: high volume with a narrow range or a dead stop in a rally or decline signals large players absorbing and standing in front of the move, so do not buy there.
claims.direction: avoid buying a rally stopped dead on high volume

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: there's a cognitive element here that has to be considered. It seems to me to be really one of the best ways to pick up this information
claims.claim: Technical analysis lacks a philosophical justification; charts (bars and candles) hold dense information through a cognitive element, which is the topic of the speaker's next book.

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: Now, of course, it's different. It's so much bigger, it seems like and it's it permeates globally.
claims.claim: The current environment resembles the 1970s (debasement, gold and silver, trend following profitable, large abrupt moves) but is bigger and global; the 200-day moving average has become more important.
claims.direction: long gold and silver, trend following up

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: Essentially the market would at the beginning would go straight up and straight down for five, six, even 10 bars in a row without taking out a low or or taking out a high
claims.claim: An early S&P pit pattern (straight runs of 5-10 five-minute bars) quadrupled an account in two months until institutions entered and compressed the market, showing how quickly an edge disappears when participants change.

claims.speaker: Toby Crabel
claims.quote: I just thought there was a better risk-adjusted return there.
claims.claim: Short-term trading gave better risk-adjusted returns and diversification versus trend following, which the speaker had done in the early 80s.
claims.testable: partly: compare Sharpe of short-term vs trend
